newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Top US envoy urges Senate to ratify chemical pact.
newsitem.headline: Top US envoy urges Senate to ratify chemical pact.

text.p: The chief U.S. negotiator for the Chemical Weapons Convention called on Monday for the Senate to ratify the stalled treaty by April 29 so Washington does not find itself in the same club as "rogue states" who reject it.

Stephen Ledogar, speaking to several reporters on his last day before retiring as U.S. ambassador to the Conference on Disarmament, said the landmark pact's verification regime was adequate to detect any "militarily-significant cheating".
On the eve of stepping down after 30 years as a U.S. career foreign service officer, the towering 67-year-old blasted unnamed critics of the pact as misinforming the U.S. public.

The Chemical Weapons Convention, ratified by 70 of the 161 countries that signed it, has been held up in the Senate Foreign Relations Committee chaired by Republican Senator Jesse Helms of North Carolina. Helms argues the treaty would be ineffective and expose U.S. chemical companies to outside inspection.
On Friday, President Bill Clinton appealed to the Republican-led Congress to approve the chemical weapons treaty aimed at preventing rogue nations from developing poison gas.

Clinton has launched a full-scale effort to gain Senate passage of the global treaty, which bans the development, production, stockpiling, transfer and use of chemical weapons. He wants it approved by an April 29 deadline when the treaty, open for signature in Paris in January 1993, takes effect.

"It is absolutely essential that the United States ratify the Chemical Weapons Convention and do so sufficiently before the April 29 so that we can deposit our instruments of ratification and be an original party," Ledogar said.

"As chief negotiator of that treaty I am appalled at some of the argumentation used by opponents of the treaty," he added. "It is so far, some of it, from being based in fact that I just don't know what document they are disparaging."
Ledogar took up the job as top U.S. negotiator at the U.N.-sponsored forum in Geneva January 1990 and saw the chemical deal clinched two years later.
"I cannot conceive how the United States would be better off outside that treaty than inside it," he said.
"We took a leadership role in the negotiation and quite frankly, the international community has a well-founded sense of betrayal that when it comes time to put it into effect that we're not there.
"We are, after all, one of the two largest chemical weapon holders," he said, referring to the Russian Federation.
"There are many others -- few of whom admit to even having programmes. But most of those others have already signed.
"If you want to get their programmes obliterated or brought to account the way to do it is working with the very significant capabilities provided for in the Chemical Weapons Convention."
Under the chemical weapons treaty, states who ratify the pact can have their facilities subject to challenge inspections.
"The CW Convention provides for verifiable, internationally binding commitments," Ledogar said. "Verifiability is not an absolute.

"Verification provided for in the CWC, in my judgement, meets an adequately high standard which I define as providing for a high probability that any militarily-significant cheating will be deterred or detected.

"I would be appalled to find that the United States winds up in the category of rogue states who have an absolutely opposite attitude toward chemical weapons than I understand that to be of my fellow Americans."

Ledogar previously headed the U.S. delegation to the Vienna negotiations on Conventional Armed Forces in Europe (1989) and was deputy chief of the U.S. mission to NATO in Brussels (1981-87). The New Yorker was also a member of the U.S. delegation to the Vietnam peace talks in Paris.
